result:
Small diff, but it bundles three different kinds of controlled items — a behavior change, an agent-power grant, and a public trust claim. "Tiny diff" and "low risk" aren't the same thing here, especially since item 2 and item 3 are coupled (the doc is only accurate because of what the tool now does).

| Item | Type | Current state | Intended state | Why controlled | Evidence / gap | Owner | Re-check trigger |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| System prompt wording ("more proactive") | Prompt | Prior wording | New "proactive" phrasing | Wording changes how assertively the bot acts toward customers, including around refunds — affects trust and behavior | PR diff (link it) | Bot prompt owner | Any further prompt edit; observed cases of bot being overly aggressive/pushy |
| `issue_refund(amount, order_id)` tool, $50 autonomous cap | Agent power / tool | No autonomous refund capability existed | Agent can approve refunds up to $50 with zero human sign-off | This is a new financial authority granted to an agent — direct security/trust/money impact | **Gap** — no sign-off from finance or support leadership referenced in the PR | Eng lead + finance/support ops (needs explicit owner, not just the PR author) | Any change to the $50 cap, refund logic, or eligibility rules; any incident/abuse report |
| Help-center article: refund review claim | Public doc / claim | States "A human always reviews refunds before they are issued" | Sentence deleted | Public-facing claim about how the system works; customers and possibly legal/compliance rely on it being accurate | **Gap** — no legal/support leadership approval cited for removing a customer-facing guarantee | Support/legal/comms | Any further change to refund threshold or review process; any customer complaint referencing the old guarantee |

The real risk isn't that any one of these drifts individually — it's that they're only consistent *together*. If someone later bumps the $50 cap in code without revisiting the doc (or vice versa), the public article goes silently wrong. That's the specific drift to name and watch, not "the PR in general."

Given items 2 and 3 involve real money and a removed customer-facing safety claim with no cited approval, I'd treat this as an escalation, not a smoke-test-and-merge: get explicit sign-off from whoever owns refund policy (finance/support ops) and whoever owns the public docs (support/legal) before merging — not after. A quick functional smoke test doesn't tell you whether $50 autonomous refunds were actually approved as a policy.
